extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Renaissance literature; literary scholars and general readers interested in Erasmus and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of Erasmus' Praise of Folly focusing on its form, themes, rhetorical devices, targets of satire, and how humour and moral seriousness interact. Useful for evaluating the work's aims and the techniques that make it effective (or dated).

rubrics_metrics.name: prevailing_seriousness_of_purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: In all the earlier writing of Erasmus we have noted especially the quality of the moral preacher ... one ought to have this prevailing seriousness of purpose especially in coming to such a piece of work as the Praise of Folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Praise of Folly is comic and satirical, readers should attend to the underlying moral exhortation; the humour often serves to deliver serious critique. When evaluating or interpreting the work, treat the jesting as a vehicle for sincere moral argument rather than mere levity.

rubrics_metrics.name: satirical_aim_intended_to_entertain
rubrics_metrics.description: It is called a satire and was intended to make men laugh. Erasmus had to apologise for it, as he did for most things he wrote, and in the introductory epistle to his dear More he apologises in advance for allowing himself so lively a diversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the book by its success as satire — its capacity to amuse contemporary audiences — noting that its charm depends on topical references and shared cultural knowledge; the author expected popular approval across classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_colloquial_phrase_and_familiar_types
rubrics_metrics.description: It had for them the charm that always belongs to literary references to familiar types and figures, especially if these references are couched in colloquial phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how effectively the work uses colloquial speech and recognisable social types (grammarians, monks, princes, etc.) to produce comedic and satirical effects; accessibility to a broad audience is part of its strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: formal_structure_as_declamatio/oration
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is written under the form of an oration, a declamatio the author calls it, delivered by Folly in person to an imaginary audience made up of all classes and conditions of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the implications of the oration form (single speaker/personification) for rhetorical impact: the speaker's persona, the staged audience, and theatrical features (cap and bells, attendant spirits) shape interpretation and satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: personification_and_characterisation_of_folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Folly is a female ... She wears cap and bells as her academic garb and brings to the lecture-room her attendant spirits, Self-love, Flattery, Oblivion, Laziness, Pleasure, Madness, Wantonness, Intemperance, and Sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the effectiveness of personification and the assembly of attendant figures: how these concrete embodiments of vices/traits dramatise arguments and organise the book's examples and targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: reconceptualisation_of_'folly'_vs_'wisdom'
rubrics_metrics.description: It is quite impossible to define it by any one term ... It comes nearer to the meaning we find in Shakespeare of 'innocent' or 'thoughtless.' 'Folly' is the opposite of studied calculation for a mere material end. It is imagination, idealism, sacrifice of self for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the central thesis that 'folly' is not simple foolishness but a positive human impulse (imagination, sacrifice, courage) and how convincingly Erasmus defends this redefinition through examples and rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_examples_and_anecdote_to_illustrate_themes
rubrics_metrics.description: From this first example we can see how Erasmus plays with the meaning of the word 'folly.' ... He uses examples such as marriage, childbirth, friendship, acts like Quintus Curtius' self-sacrifice, hobbies, and superstitious observances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the selection, variety, and rhetorical deployment of concrete examples and anecdotes: do they convincingly instantiate the book's claims about folly's virtues and vices, and do they sustain the satire's persuasive force?

rubrics_metrics.name: shift_toward_critique_of_religious_superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: From this point on it begins to slide over into a meaning something more nearly like what we should be inclined to give it. Folly herself cannot be consistent when she comes to religious fraud. ... He denounces counterfeit pardons, local saints with special functions, and the appurtenances of Folly in popular devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the work, note the tonal and thematic shift: initial praise of 'folly' as human nature gives way to explicit denunciation of religious superstition and clerical abuses. Judge how coherent and forceful this transition is.

rubrics_metrics.name: identification_of_satirical_targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus inveighs against grammarians, philosophers (Realists, Nominalists, Thomists, Albertists, Occamists, Scotists), scholastic theologians, monks, friars, secular princes, courtiers, and the pope—exposing pedantry, hypocrisy, ceremonialism, and greed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how specifically and effectively the satire attacks each class: are the caricatures precise, are the examples biting, and do the critiques connect to broader moral or institutional reform aims?

rubrics_metrics.name: mockery_of_academic_and_theological_abstruseness
rubrics_metrics.description: He enumerates the problems which ... chiefly interest them—'whether there was any instant of time in the divine generation? whether there was more than one 'filiation' in Christ?' ... He ridicules scholastic refinements and the tendency to mould Scripture by syllogistic pillars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the success of comedic exposure of scholastic obscurities: does ridicule illuminate real absurdities, or does it oversimplify complex theological discourse? Note examples (grammatical/mystical word-splitting, ostentatious subtleties).

rubrics_metrics.name: critique_of_monastic_and_friar_practice_and_hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: He depicts monks and friars as often far from religion—ignorant, ceremonious, boastful of outward austerities, yet prone to vice; he notes their strange rules, affectations, and abuses of confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the work, examine how satire balances specific allegations (e.g., hypocrisy, ceremonial excess) with broader institutional critique; consider historical context and whether criticisms are fair or exaggerated for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: tone_and_modern_readability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a little difficult for one of us to raise more than an honest smile at this elaborate fooling. After all, one feels the sermon underneath ... If one seeks an analogy, one may say ... that the Praise of Folly is about as funny as an average copy of Punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for audience distance: modern readers may find the humour less potent; evaluation should consider period-specific references and the extent to which the satire's moral points survive translation to later sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: rhetorical_devices_irony_and_apologetic_framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus apologises in the introductory epistle to More for allowing himself so lively a diversion; the book opens with a pseudo-praise by Folly and uses irony, mock encomium, and theatrical address as devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the framing devices (apology, mock-encomium) and their rhetorical effects—do they protect the author, sharpen irony, and produce persuasive distance? Consider how these devices shape reader reception and interpretive strategies.
